description: The period from 1919 to 1939 in the Indian National Movement is widely known as the Gandhian Era. During this time, Mahatma Gandhi led several nationwide mass movements based on truth and non-violence, fundamentally weakening the foundations of British Imperialism in India.

sections.title: Rise of Gandhi and Early Satyagrahas
sections.description: Mahatma Gandhi's early experiments with Satyagraha in India and the mass outrage against the draconian Rowlatt Act.

key_concepts.explanation: A technique of peaceful political resistance based on truth and non-violence, developed by Mahatma Gandhi during his struggle in South Africa.

historical_events.significance: Gandhi's First Civil Disobedience in India; launched against the exploitative Tinkathia system forced upon indigo farmers by European planters.
Gandhi's First Hunger Strike in India; mediated a dispute between textile mill owners and workers over the Plague Bonus.
Gandhi's First Non-Cooperation movement; supported peasants demanding tax remission due to severe crop failure.
General Dyer ordered indiscriminate firing on a peaceful unarmed crowd gathered in Amritsar to protest the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of local leaders Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal.

key_associations.extra_info: Popularly termed the 'Black Act'. It allowed imprisonment without trial and gave rise to the slogan 'No Vakil, No Appeal, No Dalil'.

sections.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements
sections.description: The era of remarkable Hindu-Muslim unity and the launch of the first all-India mass movement against the British government.

key_concepts.explanation: A pan-Islamic political campaign launched by Indian Muslims, led by the Ali Brothers, to protest against the dismantling of the Ottoman Empire and to restore the power of the Caliph of Turkey.

historical_events.significance: Aimed at boycotting government titles, courts, legislature, schools, and foreign goods to paralyze the British administration.
A violent mob set fire to a police station in Gorakhpur, killing 22 policemen. Deeply disturbed by the violence, Gandhi abruptly called off the Non-Cooperation Movement.

important_facts.fact: Rabindranath Tagore termed the mass burning of foreign clothes during the Non-Cooperation Movement as a 'ruthless waste'.

sections.title: Swaraj Party and Simon Commission
sections.description: The strategic shift towards council entry by the Swarajists and the nationwide boycott of British constitutional reforms.

key_concepts.explanation: The resolution for 'Complete Independence' adopted by the Indian National Congress, shifting the political goal away from mere Dominion Status.

historical_events.significance: Founded by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru to contest elections, enter legislative councils, and obstruct government functioning from within.
A 7-member statutory commission appointed for constitutional reforms. It was boycotted nationwide with 'Simon Go Back' slogans because all its members were White (no Indians were included).
The first major Indian effort to draft a constitutional framework, chaired by Motilal Nehru, which demanded Dominion Status and joint electorates.
Presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, the Congress passed the historic 'Purna Swaraj' resolution and decided to celebrate 26 January 1930 as the first Independence Day.

important_facts.fact: Veteran leader Lala Lajpat Rai succumbed to severe injuries sustained during a brutal police lathi-charge while leading a protest against the Simon Commission in Lahore.

sections.title: Civil Disobedience Movement and Round Table Conferences
sections.description: The launch of the iconic Salt Satyagraha and the subsequent constitutional negotiations held in London.

historical_events.significance: Gandhi marched 240 miles from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi with 78 followers to break the British salt monopoly, officially initiating the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Also known as the Delhi Pact; the British agreed to release political prisoners, and the Congress agreed to suspend the movement and attend the Second Round Table Conference.
Announced by British PM Ramsay MacDonald, providing separate electorates for minorities, including Muslims, Sikhs, and importantly, the Depressed Classes.
An agreement signed between Gandhi (who was fasting unto death) and B.R. Ambedkar, which replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.

key_associations.extra_info: The conference failed to achieve any substantial outcome due to the absence of India's largest political party.
Gandhi travelled to London as the sole representative of Congress on the ship SS Rajputana, but negotiations failed over the issue of minority representation.

sections.title: Government of India Act 1935 and Provincial Elections
sections.description: A major phase of constitutional restructuring and the political crisis triggered by the outbreak of the Second World War.

polity_articles.provision: Abolition of Dyarchy in provinces and introduction of Provincial Autonomy.
polity_articles.details: It introduced dyarchy at the central level and proposed an All India Federation (which never materialized). It also separated Burma from India.

historical_events.significance: Elections were held under the 1935 Act, resulting in a massive victory for the Congress, which formed ministries in 8 out of 11 provinces.
The Congress ministries resigned across all provinces after 28 months in power to protest the British Viceroy's decision to declare India a belligerent in WWII without consulting Indian leaders.
Observed by the Muslim League, led by Jinnah, to celebrate the resignation of Congress ministries. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar also supported this observance.
